findings: B and A disagree on 16% of decisions (3,329 of 20,849 in 200 games): after the same 100 PPO iterations from starts that differed in 7% of buys, the two branches have drifted apart well beyond the supervised change.

Disagreements are where B is nearly indifferent. B's margin between its top two options is the only signal with information beyond the inputs (AUC 0.60, partial r 0.16; all inputs together 0.595; the random-noise control sits at 0.50 and 0.00). Coin-flip decisions differ; confident ones do not.

They lean to the late game and to buys: 57% of divergences come after turn 12 (42% of decisions), 27% are buys (21% of decisions), 40% action decisions (44%). In 44% of them B keeps c2's choice and A moved away.

On exact values the differences are a wash. On the held-out bank, where B's and A's buys differ (431 positions over both seeds), B's buy is worth +0.26 points of win chance on average; it is clearly better in 18.8% and clearly worse in 15.8%. By phase: opening −0.05, middle +0.61, late +0.13 points. By opponent and kingdom card the groups are small and the sign changes; no card stands out with confidence.

So the verified labels did not leave a lasting, targeted advantage. This matches the promotion match: B_s2 49.9% vs frozen c2, A_s2 51.4%; head to head B led by 3.8 points on one seed and 1.2 on the other.

next_step.title: If this is tried again
next_step.text: The supervised step moved held-out decisions little (5% of verified pairs) and PPO then washed most of it out. A second attempt would need many more verified lessons (tens of thousands: 20,000 labels gave 389), or a continuing signal during PPO (search-improved targets every iteration) rather than a one-off nudge.
